https://www.dw.com/en/how-germany-suppor.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpgO Commemorations for the victims of the Berlin Pride attack started arriving mere hours after the attack Image: IMAGO/Wolfgang Maria Weber Advertisement On the evening of July 25, according to German authorities, Abdul Ballout, drove a white van into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where thousands were celebrating Berlin Pride. He then got out of the vehicle and began attacking people at random with a large knife. He killed a 65-year-old woman from Poland and injured her daughter, along with 30 other people, some of them seriously. Many details have emerged about Ballout, his links to extremists, his criminal record and his family. A day after the incident, he was shot dead by police officers while trying to flee during an arrest attempt. The identities of the victims, and how they are coping after the attack on the event celebrating LGBTQ+ rights , are not publicly known. Still, many are likely to live with its consequences for months, if not years, to come. The only details disclosed by Berlin's governing mayor concern the age and nationality of the woman who was killed. Otherwise, Germany's strict data protection laws protect victims' privacy. Victims can approach the media themselves at any time if they choose to make their stories public, Roland Weber, the German federal government's commissioner for victims of terrorism and extremist violence , told DW. Calls for political consequences after Berlin Pride attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Support for the victims In Germany , people affected by such attacks are often reluctant to come forward publicly or identify themselves as victims, said Julia Kühne. She should know: Kühne is the spokesperson for the Association for Victims of Terrorism ( VoT Germany ), which is part of an international federation of terrorism victims. "The perpetrator needs to disappear from the media, now that he has been caught and killed. Those affected should naturally be brought much more to the forefront," said Kühne. How are those who were injured in the attack doing today? Weber has visited some of them in hospital. "What I saw there was distressing. But thanks to modern medicine, and because the doctors are optimistic, there is reason for hope that everyone will recover as fully as possible," he said. "In some cases, however, that remains uncertain. Only time will tell. Some of the injured have already been discharged from hospital and are now receiving outpatient treatment. Others will begin various forms of therapy and rehabilitation." How are the victims being supported? The Federal Commissioner for Victims and Weisser Ring , a victim support organization, arrange trauma treatment , provide immediate financial assistance, and advise victims on long-term care and victims' pensions. Weisser Ring is a volunteer-run organization that works closely with the police to provide advice and support to victims of crime in Germany. "In cases of terrorist attacks, there is also a special provision: victims can apply for hardship payments," said Weber. "These are funds made available by the Bundestag. Hardly anyone knows about them, and making people aware of them is part of our job. We provide guidance and help ensure that applications are submitted as quickly as possible." Germany reviews Berlin Pride attack security failures To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Weber is also responsible for supporting the relatives of the Polish woman who was killed and her daughter, who was injured in the attack. Nationality is not a factor in this regard. He assists victims with follow-up costs and compensation whenever an act of terrorism or extremist violence has been committed on German soil. Number of traumatized victims still unclear The victims of the attack are not only those who sustained physical injuries. According to VoT Germany's Kühne, even people who witnessed the attack from several hundred meters away may be considered victims. "There are people who do not develop problems until years later," she told DW. "They may suddenly begin to suffer from sleep disturbances, experience nightmares, develop panic attacks or struggle with social phobia. In some cases, these symptoms do not emerge until years afterward because those affected were initially either still in shock or had returned to their everyday lives and were therefore able, at least to some extent, to suppress what they had experienced." Kühne also noted that survivors of previous terrorist attacks may be retraumatized by media coverage of the current attack in Berlin and find themselves in need of support once again. She knows this from personal experience: she herself survived the 2016 attack on Berlin's Christmas market, which ultimately claimed 13 lives and left more than 70 injured. In the shadow of RAF terror: The children left behind To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Victim support: Problems in practice Weisser Ring, which supports victims of crime across Germany, believes adequate compensation schemes and pension entitlements for victims of terrorism are now in place. However, not everything runs smoothly in practice, said Rolf Schmachtenberg, the organization's state chairman in Berlin. "In cases where people have suffered permanent harm, the assessment procedures are often quite lengthy," he said. "We also continue to encounter administrative bottlenecks, with some authorities still relying on paper files and fax communications. They then have to wait for information from other agencies, which can significantly delay the application process. In my view, the main problem is one of implementation." Over the past decade, Germany has experienced 13 terrorist attacks motivated by Islamist or political extremist ideologies, leaving 39 people dead and 475 injured. The support provided by the federal government's commissioner for victims has no time limit. Weber continues to assist people affected by attacks dating back to the 1980s. Commemoration continues of the nine people killed in 2020 in a racially motivated terrorist attack in the city of Hanau Image: Kadir Ilboga/Anadolu/picture alliance Victims seek answers For many victims, coming to terms with the horror and suffering also means finding answers to the question of why the perpetrator acted and why they, in particular, were targeted, said Weber. In some court proceedings, perpetrators have remained silent. In the case of the Berlin Pride attack, however, the perpetrator was killed, meaning there will never be complete clarity about his motives. In Germany, investigations are discontinued once a suspect has died. No court will ever determine whether Abdul Ballout selected his victims for one particular reason or another. "As a result, some questions will remain unanswered," said Weber. "The search for answers is something most victims have in common, but it cannot always lead to certainty." Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error. Photograph: Guardia Civil/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Investigators walking among debris at the site of the crash near Toledo. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error. Photograph: Guardia Civil/AFP/Getty Images Spain Explainer How did the Spain train crash happen and what will investigators be asking? Audio file appears to point finger at control centre, but there are questions around signalling and technical issues Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Thu 29 Oct 2026 10.39 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 69 people died when a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville hit another train on the same track from behind near Toledo on Wednesday morning. Both trains had been brought to a halt earlier when the signalling system failed. The driver of the state-owned Spanish train, a Renfe AVE service, was told by controllers to restart the journey, but crashed into the train in front, run by the private operator Iryo. The front carriages of the AVE train and rear of the Iryo train were destroyed and others derailed. How could this happen? The nature of this disaster, as well as its human toll, seems particularly shocking. There are multiple safeguards on high-speed lines, including different types of automatic train operation, which should ensure trains are never able to come close on the same track. The audio file released to Spanish media by the government appears to point the finger at the control centre, with a controller in Madrid telling the driver of the halted AVE train to proceed “ con marcha normal ” – under normal operations – rather than at low speed. The instruction was described by the transport minister, Óscar Puente, as an “inexplicable decision”. Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network Read more Has this happened before? Rear-end collisions are rare, as are any kind of crash between trains on international high-speed networks. The closest comparator occurred in China in 2011, when a high-speed train hit a stationary express in front of it in Wenzhou, killing 40 people. The rear-end collision between two East Midlands trains in Bedford this year was the first fatal crash of that kind in 40 years in the UK, and occurred on a stretch of railway without automatic train operation, after the driver apparently failed to slow despite the danger signal. What will investigators be asking? While the audio appears to indicate human error played a central role, there are other elements that remain unclear, such as what caused the initial failure of the signalling system. The German-designed train control system is being phased out and the CEO of Iryo recently told a senate inquiry that disconnection was a “frequent issue” on the line. Investigators will be looking at the sequence of events and technical issues that allowed the Renfe train to proceed but the Iryo train to stay put. ‘People were thrown in the air’: passenger recounts moment train crashed in Spain – video Signallers, or track controllers, are increasingly based in remote computer centres but are acutely aware of the risk and responsibility their job entails. Any investigation will want to establish what circumstances or pressures could have led to that instruction. In all modern hi-tech transport, whether air or rail, known safety risks are eradicated as far as possible. Accident investigations typically yield rare, if not unprecedented, combinations of technical failure and human error. ‘It all happened in a split second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain Read more What does it mean for Spain? The Spanish government will want to demonstrate that this latest disaster is completely unconnected to the head-on crash between two trains that occurred on the same line in Adamuz in January after one derailed, apparently due to a small section of faulty or missing rail. Train drivers were due to strike, even before this week’s crash, in protest against under-investment in the railway and its people, which unions say is directly connected to safety. The success of Spain’s high-speed railway, linking Madrid to Seville and Barcelona, was the envy of British rail planners. It was modern and had cut journeys from the capital to Andalusia to two and a half hours; a car takes twice that, and the public transport alternative of the coach, three times as long. Good public transportation links bring jobs and growth; losing them could mean the opposite. Are Europe’s railways safe? The long-term trend since 2010 has been fewer fatalities of any sort on the railway. Most years, in most countries, no passenger is killed in any type of train crash, a world away from the death toll on the roads. However, worries about under-investment in the railways, particularly after costs and subsidy soared as fare revenue dried up in the pandemic, are not unique to Spain. https://www.indiatimes.com/trending/why-.text: is a highly anticipated, big-budget live-action K-drama series airing on Disney+ and Hulu. The 10-episose romantic fantasy series is based on Alphatart’s web novel of the same name, which concluded its core run with 337 chapters. The web novel was later adapted into a wildly popular digital comic on Naver Webtoon. Directed by Cho Su-won and written by Yeo Ji-na, the series surprised fans with an early drop of the first four episodes, with two new episodes scheduled for every Wednesday, till the series finale on November 25, 2026. To capture the unique European architecture, etiquette, and aesthetic of the fantasy universe, the series was filmed on location in Germany and the Czech Republic, including Prague and Kutná Hora. However, the internet is less than please with the release. Despite much anticipation, the K-drama was on the receiving end of significant backlash. But why are fans dissatisfied? Here’s what we know. follows Navier Ellie Trovi, starring Shin Min-a the fiercely intelligent and perfectly poised Empress of the Eastern Empire. However, the composed and dignified Empress’ world collapses when her husband, Emperor Sovieshu, played by Ju Ji-Hoon, falls for an escaped slave named Rashta, played by Lee Se-young. The long-standing political marriage shatters when Sovieshu demands a divorce, so he can place Rashta on the throne. Things take a turn, when instead of wallowing in self-pity and heartbreak, Navier agrees to the divorce. But the agreement comes at the cost of a political bombshell, the approval to remarry Prince Heinrey, the enigmatic and devoted leader of the rival Western Kingdom. Lee Jong-suk plays Prince Heinrey Alles Lazlo. Navier would go any length to outmanoeuvre her ex-husband and regain her throne, and in doing so she forges an unlikely alliance with Prince Heinrey. Reactions to the first few episodes have revealed that the ambitious project has failed to deliver the premise it had promised. Several netizens took to social media to express their dissatisfaction towards the series. The major criticism was directed at the production and quality of the K-drama. An X user wrote, “Why the remarried empress literally be looking like some Instagram reel drama what’s up with production.” Similar responses: Others had a few choice words to say about the cast. One user wrote, “This needed younger actors tbh”, while another shared, “The actress playing Navier looks far too old for the role. Plus, her overall aesthetic doesn’t complement Henry’s, who looks young and charming. I sense absolutely no chemistry between Navier and Henry. Terrible casting.” Another viral tweet also criticised Joo Ji-hoon for his looks. Some also slammed the costumes. One X user wrote, “Whoever was in charge of the costumes should probably take a long break because what exactly are those outfits? Especially the actress’s costumes. The designs are just not giving what they’re supposed to give. Such a disappointment.” has sparked a wave of opinions from netizens. While fans of the original novel and the Webtoon expressed their dissatisfaction over the adaptation, others await further episode releases. It remains to be seen whether the K-drama can turn public opinion around.

https://www.dw.com/en/coalition-of-the-w.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PZ9I Prefer DW on Google The 'Coalition of the Willing' comprises European countries as well as EU and NATO leaders Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Sven Simon/picture alliance Advertisement Once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter. Extensive security measures have already been announced for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets. The "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now. DW interview with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London. But what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic. "The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no plan outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises." Merz: 'Germany has a seat at the table' Nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward. Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine. Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice. This has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)? After the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz said: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear." Europe has yet to speak with one voice But what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part. Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate says a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under. "Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister said. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that." German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator. At the federal government's regular press briefing, he said: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place." Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video German government spokesperson: Europe now needs stamina US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump , struck a rather different tone last week. Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he said: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations." Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question." Hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about. Declining support for Ukraine in German polls European supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the issue is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly. According to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the issue, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war. A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing issue in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine. This article was originally written in German.
